label: Painting

label: Stratigraphy

label: Figure–ground (perception)

label: Photographic processing

prior_cards.card: Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa, also called The Great Wave, is a Japanese woodblock print in Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Examining its ink-and-color medium alongside the museum’s other impressions opens an exploration of the relationship between a print design and individual printed sheets.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a named woodblock design from the individual impressions through which it is encountered.

prior_cards.card: Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa places Mount Fuji inside the hollow of a towering wave, making the mountain look unexpectedly small. Part of Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, this woodblock design uses perspective to make scale and visual importance diverge within one dramatic composition.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: See how Hokusai’s composition makes Mount Fuji look small inside a looming wave.

label: History
description: past events and their documentation, studied through historiography, archaeology, and related disciplines

prior_cards.card: History investigates the human past through surviving objects, writing, and oral traditions. These traces require interpretation: accounts can change when evidence is questioned or new perspectives are considered. A diary, an artifact, and a later historian’s argument can therefore answer different questions about the same past.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Treat accounts of the past as evidence-based interpretations that can change.

label: Visual arts
description: practice of art which creates works that are primarily visual in nature

label: Faux painting
description: painting technique used to imitate the look of other materials such as wood, marble, or fabric

label: Literature
description: polysemous term referring to a written art form, and the set of all literary works

label: Hinduism
description: religion widely practiced in the Indian subcontinent

label: Typology (archaeology)
description: classification of archaeological artifacts according to their physical characteristics

label: Photography
description: Creating images with cameras through choices of light, composition and timing.

prior_cards.card: Photography creates images by recording light, using processes ranging from light-sensitive paper to electronic sensors. A photogram makes this relationship concrete: objects placed directly on sensitive material block some of the light, creating an image without a camera or lens.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Explore light recording through the contrast between sensor images and camera-free photograms.

label: Oral history
description: Recording and interpreting people's firsthand accounts of past experiences.

prior_cards.card: Oral history records people’s accounts of the past through interviews. Memories are shaped by later experience, and the interviewer helps shape what is told. Exploring consent, careful questioning, and preservation reveals how a conversation becomes a historical source.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Understand how recorded recollections become evidence while retaining the context and agency of their narrators.

label: Archaeology
description: Understanding past societies through material remains and landscapes.

prior_cards.card: Archaeology investigates human lives through physical remains, from stone tools to recent buildings. An object’s location and its relationship to other finds help explain past activities. Explore how recording that context helps reconstruct activities that written records may overlook.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Explain why archaeological context is necessary for interpreting a find.

label: Printmaking
description: Producing images through prepared surfaces and transferred impressions.

label: Sculpture
description: Creating three-dimensional forms from physical materials.

label: Color theory
description: Exploring how colors interact perceptually and compositionally.

prior_cards.card: Color theory explores relationships among colors in art and design. On a traditional painter’s color wheel, complementary pairs sit opposite each other. Comparing neighboring blue and orange areas offers a concrete example of how surrounding colors can make each other appear more intense.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Explore complementary colors as a relationship within a particular color-wheel model.

label: Poetry
description: Creating and interpreting writing shaped by rhythm, imagery and language.

label: Christianity
description: Exploring Christian beliefs, practices, institutions and histories.

label: Islam
description: Exploring Islamic beliefs, practices, institutions and histories.

label: Judaism
description: Exploring Jewish religious traditions, practices and intellectual histories.

label: Buddhism
description: Exploring Buddhist traditions, communities, teachings and practices.

label: Shinto
description: Exploring Japanese religious traditions associated with kami and ritual life.

label: Cartography
description: Designing maps to represent spatial information.

prior_cards.card: Cartography combines scientific methods, design and technology to make and use maps. A map selects features and represents them with symbols rather than reproducing everything in a place. Exploring these choices reveals how a map communicates particular spatial relationships to its readers.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Recognize mapmaking as purposeful selection and representation of spatial information.

label: Cultural landscapes
description: Examining landscapes shaped by relationships between people and environments.

prior_cards.card: Cultural landscapes reflect sustained relationships between people and their natural surroundings. They include designed gardens, cultivated terraces and places valued for spiritual associations. Exploring how a landscape was shaped, used and understood over time reveals cultural history in the visible environment.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Read landscapes as evidence of changing relationships between people and nature.

prior_cards.card: Etching lets acid do the cutting. An artist scratches a design through an acid-resistant coating on a metal plate; acid then bites the exposed lines. Longer exposure deepens them. After the coating is removed, those incisions provide the image for an intaglio print.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Follow how acid converts lines drawn through a protective ground into printable grooves.

prior_cards.card: In Gérard Genette’s framework, focalization concerns which information a narrative makes available. A story may restrict itself to one character’s knowledge even when someone else narrates. Separating access to information from the identity of the speaker makes narrative viewpoint more precise than a first-person/third-person label.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Separate restrictions on narrative information from the identity of the speaker.

prior_cards.card: Narrative metalepsis crosses the boundary between telling a story and inhabiting it. A narrator might enter the action, or a fictional character might intrude into the narrator’s world. Such crossings can produce comic or fantastic effects by disturbing levels that the narrative normally keeps separate.
prior_cards.learning_takeaway: Notice crossings between the level of telling and the world being told.
